summary: LunarWindow is a browser-based tool for comparing lunar landing sites and dates in seconds. Pick a site (Apollo, CLPS, Chandrayaan-3, Chang'e, or the Artemis south-pole regions) or type in coordinates, then choose a landing date. LunarWindow shows where the Sun and Earth sit relative to the local horizon, how long until sunset and Earthset, what share of the mission has sunlight and a direct-to-Earth radio link, and a GO / MARGINAL / NO-GO verdict. When a launch slips, planners can shift the date by a day, a week or a lunar month, see the best landing windows over the next 60 days, and compare scenarios side by side. Today that takes several specialist tools. Here it's a single click.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

LunarWindow is a browser tool that lets mission planners, educators and the public compare lunar landing sites and dates in seconds. Pick a site (Apollo, CLPS, Chandrayaan-3, Chang'e, SLIM, or the Artemis south-pole regions) or enter any coordinates, choose a landing time, and LunarWindow shows:

- Sun and Earth elevation and azimuth at touchdown, compared with the local horizon

- Time until sunset or sunrise, and until Earthset or Earthrise

- Percentage of the mission with sunlight, with a direct-to-Earth radio link, and with both at once

- Longest dark spell (how long the battery must last) and longest communication gap

- An energy index for vertical Sun-tracking, flat, or 2-axis solar panels

- A feasibility score and a GO / MARGINAL / NO-GO verdict, with the reasons spelled out

VISUALS

- A 360-degree sky view from the lander, stretched vertically to show how the Sun and Earth skim the horizon near the pole

- A timeline of height above the local horizon, with sunlight and Earth-link bands, a draggable cursor and Play animation

- A "best landing dates" chart that scores every 3-hour landing slot over the next 60 days; click a bar to jump to that date

- A side-by-side scenario comparison table that highlights the best value in each column, copyable as CSV

HOW IT WORKS

All calculations run in the browser with no server or internet connection needed. The Moon's position uses the lunar theory in Meeus, Astronomical Algorithms (chapter 47), and libration (the Moon's wobble) uses chapter 53. Together they give the points on the Moon directly beneath the Sun and the Earth. From those, the app calculates the azimuth and elevation seen from the landing site, including Earth's parallax and the size of the Sun's disc. The Moon has no atmosphere, so there is no refraction: the horizon is the local terrain, lowered by the Moon's curvature when the lander stands above its surroundings. Users can set a horizon elevation or paste a horizon profile, for example one derived from LOLA data.

BENEFITS

- When hardware delays or launch slips happen, engineers can test alternative dates at the same site, or nearby sites on the same date, in seconds instead of working through several specialist tools.

- Science and engineering teams see the same numbers for power, communications and survival.

- Students and the public can see why the south pole is so hard: the Sun never rises more than about 1.5 degrees there, and Earth moves up and down with libration.

ACCURACY

Sun elevations computed for the Apollo 11, 12, 15 and 17 landings match published values within about 0.1 degrees, and libration matches Meeus' worked example 53.a. Limitations: terrain is modelled as a horizon profile rather than full LOLA ray-tracing, and the coordinates for south-pole candidate regions are approximate.

TOOLS

HTML, CSS, JavaScript (no frameworks), HTML Canvas. Hosted as a single static file on GitHub Pages.

SI DISCLOSURE: Most of the application code and this project text were generated with Claude (Anthropic), an AI assistant. I chose the challenge, directed the features and scoring approach, and tested and validated the results against Apollo landing data. The app's footer and page metadata, and the demo slides, carry the same disclosure. No NASA logos or branding were used.
